name: Tulobuterol

lead: Tulobuterol is a long-acting beta-2 agonist delivered through a skin patch, approved in Japan since 1998 for asthma and COPD.
In fat-loss discussions it is mentioned alongside other beta agonists that people associate with a leaner look. Its published research is entirely about breathing conditions.

paras: It stimulates beta-2 adrenergic receptors, relaxing airway muscle. The patch releases the drug slowly, peaking around 9 to 12 hours after application, which smooths blood levels.
Typical beta-2 agonist effects include tremor and palpitations. It is a prescription drug where approved and is on lists of beta-agonists screened for in testing programmes.

chain: Beta agonists are associated with raised metabolic rate and fat mobilisation
angle.text: People discuss tulobuterol as a milder, patch-delivered member of the beta-agonist family used for cutting. Its approved use is bronchodilation; the fat-loss idea is an extrapolation from the drug class.

lead: Tulobuterol is a beta-2 adrenergic agonist best known as the active ingredient in a once-daily skin patch (Hokunalin Tape), the first bronchodilator available as a transdermal patch, approved in Japan in 1998 for asthma and COPD.[1] In looksmaxxing and fat-loss circles it is discussed as a patch-form relative of clenbuterol-type beta agonists, which people associate with fat loss and a leaner look; the route from the drug to a leaner appearance is by extrapolation from the beta-agonist class rather than from tulobuterol-specific data.

The patch releases the drug slowly so that peak blood level coincides with the early-morning dip in lung function while avoiding high peaks that cause systemic side effects.[1] Pharmacokinetic work found a lag of about 4 hours after application and a peak at roughly 9 to 12 hours.[2] A survey of 1,470 patients found that 83.2% of transdermal users with asthma reported taking treatment as prescribed, against 52.7% of inhaler users.[3]
Published research is medical: asthma, COPD, cough and perioperative breathing events in children. No published study found examines tulobuterol for body composition.

sections.h: Use in fat-loss and physique circles
paras: Tulobuterol appears in fat-loss discussions because it belongs to the family of beta-2 agonists, a group that includes clenbuterol and that bodybuilders and cutting-phase dieters associate with increased metabolic rate and fat mobilisation. Proponents of this reasoning present the patch as a gentler, steadier-release option than oral beta agonists, since its design avoids sharp peaks in blood level.[1] The chain they describe runs from receptor stimulation to higher energy expenditure to a leaner body composition.

No clinical study of tulobuterol for fat loss or muscle gain has been published. Its documented effects concern airway smooth muscle, and the body-composition idea remains a hypothesis drawn from other drugs in the class.[1][4]

The patch is prescribed in Japan for bronchial asthma and COPD, applied once daily.[1] A 2001 Japanese review noted that the tulobuterol tape was then the only long-acting beta-2 stimulant in use in Japan alongside inhaled salmeterol and formoterol, and that once-daily tape and twice-daily inhalers were each reported to give stable bronchodilation over 24 hours.[5] It has been used for nocturnal and early-morning symptoms, and trials have combined it with the inhaled anticholinergic tiotropium in COPD.[6][7] A bioequivalence study compared the Bretol and Hokunalin 2 mg patches in healthy volunteers.[8]

Other trials include a placebo-controlled study of the patch for respiratory adverse events in 188 children undergoing tonsillectomy, and a study in young children with acute asthma exacerbations.[9][10] Pediatric reviews list tulobuterol among the transdermal patches used in children.[11] An older two-month trial compared tulobuterol aerosol with fenoterol aerosol in chronic obstructive lung disease.[12]

Tulobuterol stimulates beta-2 adrenergic receptors, relaxing airway smooth muscle.[1] The skin patch is designed so that the absorbed drug reaches its highest concentration in the morning hours, matching the daily dip in lung function, and so that blood levels do not rise excessively, which reduces systemic reactions.[1] Studies of skin permeability have compared formulations of the patch and how well they follow the skin.[13]

After transdermal application in healthy volunteers there was an absorption lag of about 4 hours, with Cmax and AUC rising linearly with dose and a tmax of about 9 to 12 hours; after inhalation absorption was rapid.[2] Tulobuterol is a non-catechol beta-2 agonist, so it is not broken down by MAO or COMT; in humans it is conjugated mainly with sulfate.[14]

A 1985 review notes that common adverse effects of beta-2 agonists, such as tremor and tachycardia, are extensions of their pharmacology and do not differ markedly between agents at equipotent doses.[4] The transdermal design aims to reduce their incidence by avoiding peak concentrations.[1]

Tulobuterol has the formula C12H18ClNO and is described in encyclopedic sources as marketed in Japan as Hokunalin tape, approved in several countries and available by prescription only.[15] Analytical chemistry papers list tulobuterol among the beta-agonists screened for in urine and meat samples,[16] which is the context in which it appears in residue and anti-doping style testing methods.

Randomized and registered studies cover COPD with tiotropium, acute asthma in young children, bioequivalence of two patches, and perioperative respiratory events in children undergoing tonsillectomy (188 participants randomised to tulobuterol or placebo in a triple-blinded trial).[6][7][8][9][10][17][18] An adherence survey of 1,470 patients compared inhaled drugs with the patch.[3] No studies on fat loss or body composition were found.
